content: Fuchs' dystrophy, pronounced as Fooks, is a progressive eye condition in which the cells lining the inner surface of the cornea, known as the endothelium, gradually die off. This disease typically affects both eyes. Symptoms of Fuchs' Dystrophy: Patients may experience eye pain. There is often an increased sensitivity to light, particularly glare. Vision may appear foggy or blurred, especially in the mornings. Some individuals report seeing colored halos around lights. Vision tends to worsen progressively throughout the day. Causes of Fuchs' Dystrophy: The disease targets the endothelial layer of the cornea, which is responsible for pumping excess fluid out of the cornea. As endothelial cells die, fluid accumulates in the cornea, leading to swelling and cloudiness. Initially, fluid buildup may occur only during sleep when the eyes are closed. Over time, the condition worsens, and small blisters may form on the endothelial layer. These blisters can enlarge and rupture, causing significant eye pain. The disease may also alter the shape of the cornea, further impairing vision. The exact cause of Fuchs' dystrophy remains unknown. Risk Factors: Fuchs' dystrophy can be inherited, often in an autosomal dominant pattern. If one parent has the condition, there is a 50% chance of passing it on to their children. However, the disease can also occur in individuals without a family history. Women are more commonly affected than men. Symptoms typically do not manifest until after the age of 50, although early signs may be detectable in individuals in their 30s or 40s. Diagnosis: A slit-lamp examination performed by an ophthalmologist can confirm the diagnosis. Additional diagnostic tests may include: Pachymetry: Specular microscopy: Examines the endothelial cell layer. Visual acuity testing: Assesses the clarity of vision. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if you experience: Eye pain. Sensitivity to light. A sensation of a foreign object in the eye when none is present. Vision disturbances, such as halos or cloudiness. Progressive worsening of vision. Treatment Options: Eye drops or ointments that reduce corneal fluid can alleviate symptoms. If painful sores develop on the cornea, soft contact lenses or surgical procedures to create protective flaps over the sores may help reduce discomfort. The only definitive cure for Fuchs' dystrophy is a corneal transplant. This condition is one of the leading indications for corneal transplantation in the United States. An alternative to traditional corneal transplantation is Deep Lamellar Keratoplasty (DLK), where only the deeper layers of the cornea are replaced with donor tissue. This procedure does not require stitches, has a faster recovery time, and carries a lower risk of complications such as tissue rejection. Prognosis: Fuchs' dystrophy is a progressive condition that worsens over time. Without a corneal transplant, severe cases can lead to blindness, significant pain, and profound vision loss. Mild cases may deteriorate following cataract surgery. Surgeons may adjust their techniques or timing to minimize this risk. Potential Complications: Increased sensitivity to light. Vision loss, ranging from mild to severe. Frequent and intense eye pain as the disease advances. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent Fuchs' dystrophy. Avoiding cataract surgery or taking specific precautions during such procedures may help slow the progression of the disease.
